# The Quiet Conversation Between Who You Were and Who You've Become

There's a particular kind of reverie that strikes you at strange hours — not nostalgia exactly, but something more disorienting. You're standing in a kitchen, washing a plate, and suddenly you remember a version of yourself that made entirely different choices. You remember liking different things. You remember a morning you once woke up and felt absolutely certain about something you now find ridiculous.

The person who lived in that body, who wore those clothes, who laughed at those jokes — they were you, and they're also someone you can't fully access anymore. It's like having a friendship with someone who moved to another country decades ago. You carry fragments of them. A mannerism. A habit of speech. A preference for rainy weather or garlic in everything you cook. But the full person? That's already gone, dissolved into the sediment of subsequent years.

We don't talk enough about how strange it is that a person can change so thoroughly while remaining technically continuous. There's no moment of transformation. No dramatic overnight metamorphosis. One day you're the kid who thought two hundred dollars was a fortune and the next day you're the adult who spent four hundred dollars on a lamp and felt vaguely okay about it. The transition happened somewhere in the blur of ordinary Tuesdays.

What fascinates me about this is the question of ownership. When you make a decision at age nineteen — to move, to leave, to commit to something or abandon something — that decision was made by someone with limited information, limited perspective, and a brain that was still literally not finished growing. And yet that person gets to make choices that the rest of you has to live with for decades. The twenty-two-year-old signs a lease. The twenty-five-year-old starts a relationship. The thirty-year-old passes on an opportunity. Each version of you makes a bet, and every subsequent version inherits the consequences without having been consulted.

This is, I think, one of the underappreciated challenges of being alive. We treat memory as a stable archive — a filing cabinet we can reach into and retrieve the past — but memory is more like a story we keep rewriting. Every time you remember something, you're not pulling a document from a drawer. You're reconstructing an event through the lens of everything you've become since. The birthday party feels different now than it did then because the person remembering it is different now than the person who lived it. The ache or the joy of the recollection belongs more to your present self than to your past self.

This has implications for how we forgive people, including ourselves. Much of the cruelty people inflict — the words said in anger, the abandonment, the selfishness — comes from people who didn't yet understand something they understand now. Or perhaps more accurately, came from people who understood something entirely different. You can't really judge someone for a choice they made with a brain and a heart that no longer exist in the same configuration. It's a bit like holding a painting responsible for being made by an artist who later became a sculptor.

And yet, we do. We hold people — and ourselves — accountable not for who they are but for who they were. The version of someone that lives in our memory gets frozen like an insect in amber, and we argue with that frozen version while the living, breathing person has moved on in ways we may not have noticed.

There's a passage in some book I once read — I can't recall which — about how you meet people in layers. The first time you see someone, you see the surface: their face, their posture, the sound of their voice. Over time, you see deeper layers — their fears, their contradictions, the things they do when they think no one is watching. But there's an even deeper layer, one that most people never show anyone, which is the layer of all the versions they've already outgrown. The disappointments. The abandoned selves. The versions they're embarrassed by.

I think the bravest thing a person can do is to acknowledge that they are not the same person they were five years ago — and to extend that same understanding to everyone around them. Most conflict, most resentment, most heartbreak is rooted in the refusal to accept this simple truth. People change. They change so gradually that you don't notice, and then one day you look up and realize you've been talking to a stranger wearing a familiar face.

But here's what I keep coming back to: this impermanence isn't tragic. It's actually the most hopeful thing about being alive. The fact that you are not fixed, that you are not finished, that the person you were twenty years ago would be amazed by the person you've become — this means you're still in motion. You're still becoming. Every layer you shed, every version you outgrow, is proof that life is still doing something with you.

The kitchen plate is clean. The water is off. And somewhere in the quiet, a version of yourself from long ago looks at you and doesn't quite recognize what you've become — but is, perhaps, relieved.
